title: Notification service
summary: Fan-out to push, email and SMS with priorities and retries.
prompt: Design a service other teams call to notify users by push, email and SMS. It must respect user preferences and quiet hours, keep one-time login codes fast during marketing blasts, and survive provider outages.

requirements: Functional: accept a send request (user, template, data, priority), apply opt-outs and quiet hours, deliver by push, email or SMS, and report status per channel.
Non-functional: at-least-once delivery with few duplicates, absorbs bursts, and transactional messages stay fast regardless of bulk load.
Clarify: scheduled sends, localisation, and whether marketing and transactional traffic share capacity.
estimation: 50M daily users × 5 notifications ≈ 250M a day ≈ 3,000/s on average.
A campaign of 10M messages released over a few minutes is ~50,000/s, so queue it and drain at provider-safe rates.
At ~1 KB of delivery log per message: 250 GB a day, about 7.5 TB for 30 days of history.
api: POST /notifications {idempotencyKey, userId, template, data, priority, channels?, sendAt?} → 202 {notificationId}.
GET /notifications/{id} → status per channel: queued, sent, delivered, failed or suppressed.
GET and PUT /users/{id}/preferences: per category and channel, plus quiet hours and time zone.
data: notifications(id, caller, idempotency_key, user_id, template, payload, priority, created_at), unique on (caller, idempotency_key).
deliveries(notification_id, channel, attempt, provider_message_id, status, updated_at) as an append-only log.
preferences(user_id, category, channel, enabled) and devices(user_id, push_token, platform, last_seen).
design: The API validates and stores the request, then publishes to a queue for its priority (transactional or bulk).
Router workers load preferences, render the template, delay messages that fall in quiet hours, and fan out to per-channel queues.
Channel senders call providers with timeouts and retries (exponential backoff with jitter); provider callbacks update delivered and bounced status.
deepDives: Duplicates: the idempotency key makes the API safe to retry. Senders record each attempt and pass a provider idempotency key where supported. A crash between sending and recording can still duplicate, so keep that window small; exactly-once to a phone is not achievable.
Isolation: separate queues and worker pools per priority and channel, so a marketing blast can never delay login codes.
Provider failover: a circuit breaker per provider; on sustained errors, route email or SMS to a secondary provider.
bottlenecks: Preference lookups on every message: cache them with a short TTL and invalidate on update.
Dead push tokens: delete tokens that providers report as invalid.
Poison messages: after N attempts move them to a dead-letter queue and alert, instead of retrying forever.
tradeoffs: At-least-once delivery with deduplication is cheaper and more available than chasing exactly-once.
Quiet hours trade timeliness for user trust; security codes bypass them.
Per-channel queues add moving parts but give independent scaling and failure isolation.

rubric.text: Applied preferences, opt-outs and quiet hours before sending.
Separated transactional from bulk traffic so bursts cannot starve critical messages.
Used retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue.
Designed for at-least-once delivery with idempotency to limit duplicates.
Tracked per-channel status, including provider callbacks.
Planned provider failover and per-provider rate limits.
Defined metrics and alerts: delivery rate, latency by priority, dead-letter depth.
